This matches my own experience, pre-AI. As I've moved from IC to having a team over the years, more code was being written than I could possibly understand at the depth I would have if I'd written it myself.

The skill I learned is exactly as you describe: understand the system. For me, this means "boxes and lines", the components and how they interact. I've encouraged developers on my team to make sequence diagrams part of their deliverable, because it helps both of us put the code in the context of the system.

The boxes can be opaque because I know the boundaries and expected inputs and outputs. This tells me when I need to go in a box: is it sending a malformed message? I can trace that back into the code.

I think that's the skill we have to cultivate now that coding agents produce far more than we can review line-by-line. The system view is the map, and the boundaries tell us where to go hunting inside the box.

No, it’s not equivalent to managing a team, because the AI has no skin in the game.

A decision an AI makes is not equivalent to a decision a human makes because the consequences are not equivalent. An AI cannot be fired; cannot be sexually rejected; cannot disappoint its loved ones; cannot spend a cold night on the streets. A human who makes decisions with complete disregard to material consequences is a human you need to get off your team ASAP because they’re a ticking time bomb: a liability.

So, in building your systems, you need to be sensitive and aware to the fact that AI has no skin in the game.

I like the analogy. It feels right. But I don't think it actually is, because it leans hard on the _feeling_ of failure, vs. the actual failure.

The failure that actually matters here is product failure. Angry users. Security incidents. Downtime. Broken workflows.

Stressed and uncomfortable developers have, historically, been a leading indicator of product failure. Software is complex and when devs can't handle the breadth of ownership + the depth of expertise at the same time, it means bad work that leads to product failure. It's not clear that agents fail in the same way, or that our collective intuition about how and when to trust agents is sufficiently developed to predict product failure in the same way.

As anecdata: I know a bunch of growth-SaaS/last-batch-of-IPO companies where the devs are all stressed, the feature ship rate is up, and incidents are down. All at the same time.

So yes, quick learners and just-in-time depth is important, but so is intuition about where discomfort is going to produce true failure. The discomfort isn't a feeling to throw away, simply trusting that you'll learn everything in time. Ownership requires holding a model of the system in your head and proactively steering where you dive.

I always build a massive testing harness. I care about correctness, of course, and that is normally dealt with by the AI without having to ask. If you ask for a function, it will write tests.

But I also care about the complexity classes of the solution. I prod it about the time and space complexity, and about cache locality.

I do a lot of black box testing: take the solution, see if it does what I expected, then bake in those expectations in a document.

I find that if I do those things, it produces better code than I could do in the same time.

I also think it's more or less the same as how I used to work, just more thorough and with fewer time-consuming, trivial bugs.
